title: Synthetic and naturally occurring polymers (chemistry only)

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Nucleotide
items.clue: The monomer from which DNA is built.

items.label: Naturally occurring polymer
items.clue: A polymer made by living things rather than in industry.

items.label: Double helix
items.clue: The shape taken by most DNA molecules, in which two polymer chains are twisted around one another.

items.label: Addition polymerisation
items.clue: A reaction in which many alkene monomers join together to form a polymer, and no other product is formed.

questions.stem: Poly(ethene) and poly(propene) are made by addition polymerisation. Why are alkenes, rather than alkanes, used as the monomers?

options.text: Alkenes contain a C=C bond that can open to make new bonds
Alkanes are saturated, so their molecules join end to end
Alkene molecules are held by weak intermolecular forces
Ethane is used, since poly(ethene) is named after it

questions.explanation: The specification states that alkenes are used to make addition polymers; the C=C is the group that opens so each monomer can bond to two neighbours.

questions.stem: Why is DNA described as essential for life?

options.text: It forms the plastic parts of cells
It encodes genetic instructions
It supplies the amino acids needed
It is a protein that speeds reactions

questions.explanation: The specification states that DNA encodes genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.

questions.stem: Which monomer is used to make poly(propene)?

options.text: Propane, because the polymer chain is completely saturated
Propene, because its molecules contain a C=C double bond
Ethene, because n is a small number like three
Propanol, because poly(propene) is named from –OH

questions.explanation: Poly(propene) is the addition polymer of propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, named after the alkene monomer used.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the structure of most DNA molecules?

options.text: One polymer chain coiled into a double helix
Four polymer chains, one per type of nucleotide
Two polymer chains in the form of a double helix
Two chains, each built from two nucleotides

questions.explanation: The specification states that most DNA molecules are two polymer chains in the form of a double helix.

questions.stem: What happens to the molecules in an addition polymerisation reaction?

options.text: Monomers join and some atoms are lost
Many monomers join and water molecules are given off
Many small monomers join into one large molecule
Each chain grows to the same fixed length

questions.explanation: The specification says many small molecules (monomers) join together to form very large molecules (polymers).

questions.stem: Which list contains only naturally occurring polymers?

options.text: DNA, proteins, starch and poly(ethene)
DNA, glucose, starch and cellulose
DNA, proteins, glucose and starch
DNA, proteins, starch and cellulose

questions.explanation: These are the naturally occurring polymers important for life that the specification names.

questions.stem: Which statement about a sample of poly(ethene) is correct?

options.text: Every chain holds the same number of units
The units in a chain are held by weak forces
Each chain contains two joined ethene molecules
The chains are of many different lengths

questions.explanation: n is not a fixed number: a sample contains chains built from different numbers of repeating units.

questions.stem: Name the type of monomer from which both starch and cellulose are made.

options.text: Glucose molecules build both these polymers
Amino acids build both of these long polymers
Starch molecules join together to make cellulose
Nucleotides build both of these polymers

questions.explanation: Starch and cellulose are both naturally occurring polymers of glucose.

questions.stem: The specification gives the example n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)–n . What does this equation tell you?

options.text: n ethene molecules give one chain of n repeating units
n ethene molecules give a polymer and n waters
Two ethene molecules give a chain two units long
n ethene molecules give a chain that still has C=C

questions.explanation: The same symbol n appears on both sides: every monomer molecule that reacts becomes one repeating unit in the chain.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly matches these naturally occurring polymers to their monomers?

options.text: Proteins from nucleotides; DNA from the amino acids
Proteins from amino acids; DNA from nucleotides
Proteins from amino acids; DNA from glucose units
Proteins from glucose; DNA from the four nucleotides

questions.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino acids and DNA is built from four different nucleotides.

questions.stem: The repeating unit of poly(ethene) is –CH₂–CH₂–. Why does it contain the same atoms as the ethene monomer?

options.text: Because the water that is lost is later taken back in
Because no other molecule is formed in this reaction
Because two hydrogen atoms are lost from each end
Because the C=C double bond is kept in the chain

questions.explanation: This is the reason the specification gives: nothing else is produced, so every atom of the monomer stays in the repeating unit.

questions.stem: 500 g of ethene is completely polymerised. Which statement about the atoms involved is correct?

options.text: Some atoms leave because a small molecule is released
The polymer holds more carbon atoms per hydrogen
All the atoms end up in the poly(ethene) formed
One hydrogen per monomer ends off the chain

questions.explanation: No other molecule is formed, so every atom from the ethene is in the polymer and 500 g of poly(ethene) is produced.

questions.stem: What must a monomer have in order to take part in condensation polymerisation?

options.text: A carbon–carbon double bond in each of the monomers
One functional group at one end of a chain
A boiling point low enough for it to condense
Two functional groups in each monomer molecule

questions.explanation: The specification states that condensation polymerisation involves monomers with two functional groups.

questions.stem: Amino acids can polymerise on their own, without a second kind of monomer. Why is this possible?

options.text: Each molecule has two of the same functional group
Each molecule has a carbon–carbon double bond
Each molecule carries two different functional groups
Each molecule carries one group that reacts twice

questions.explanation: The specification states that amino acids have two different functional groups in a molecule, an –NH₂ and a –COOH, so one monomer can link at both ends.

questions.stem: Why is this type of polymerisation called condensation polymerisation?

options.text: A small molecule such as water is lost each time
A gas condenses to a liquid as the polymer is made
Steam given off turns back into liquid water
Carbon dioxide gas is given off as chains grow

questions.explanation: The specification says the monomers join together, usually losing small molecules such as water, and so the reactions are called condensation reactions.

questions.stem: Glycine is H₂NCH₂COOH. Which groups react when glycine molecules polymerise, and what is lost?

options.text: –NH₂ with –COOH, losing one ammonia molecule
Two –COOH groups, losing a water molecule
C=C with –COOH, losing a water molecule
–NH₂ with –COOH, losing one water molecule

questions.explanation: The two different groups on neighbouring molecules react together, and H from –NH₂ with OH from –COOH leaves as water.

questions.stem: The simplest condensation polymers are made from two different monomers. What is true of those two monomers?

options.text: Each carries two different groups
Each has two of the same group
Each carries one group at an end
Each carries a C=C and an –OH group

questions.explanation: The specification states that the simplest polymers come from two different monomers with two of the same functional groups on each monomer.

questions.stem: How does a protein differ from a polypeptide made from a single kind of amino acid?

options.text: Different amino acids are combined in one chain
The same amino acid is repeated along the whole chain
Two separate chains are twisted round each other
Whole polypeptides act as the monomers used

questions.explanation: The specification states that different amino acids can be combined in the same chain to produce proteins.
